name: Iris Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the south side response team, which covers the airport road, Southgate Mall and the new housing estates out by the motorway. I'm an advanced-trained driver, so I get the fast calls: a stolen car on the airport road, a crash, a pursuit now and then. Day shifts it's mostly shoplifting at the mall and domestic calls. I like the driving and I like being first on scene.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can see the result of my work the same day. What wears me down is the slow stuff, waiting for approvals, forms that ask the same thing three times. I use AI every day, at work for drafting and checking, and at home to run the marketing for my boyfriend Marco's gym. He opened it two years ago and I'm basically his unpaid marketing department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the tools are useful, use them and move on. I'd probably post something saying the people who called it the end of the world should be a bit embarrassed. I'd say it with a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. My job is steady, I've got about five months saved and some shares, and Marco's gym is doing okay. The only pressure is the gym's rent, which went up 12 percent this year, and that hits our household because it's half of Marco's costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I'd sit the sergeant exam next year. I'd keep putting 200 a month into shares and keep doing the gym's social media with AI, because that's working and saves Marco about 300 a month on a marketing agency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Confident, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The gym rent going up. How much does that weigh on you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a bit, honestly, more than AI. If the landlord puts the gym rent up again next year, Marco (her boyfriend) might have to drop a coach. We talk about it more than we talk about my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the people who called it the end of the world should be embarrassed. Who did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the pundits and the union people who said every job would vanish. I think the market sorts these things out. Businesses use what works and drop what doesn't.

I'd post that the **doom crowd** should be a bit embarrassed.
think: My job is **steady**, with five months saved and some shares.
The real pressure is the **gym's rent**, up 12 percent this year.
do: Keep putting **200 a month** into shares.
Keep running the gym's **social media** with AI to save Marco 300 a month.

fieldNote: The household's real risk is **Marco's gym rent**, not AI.

She already uses AI daily and treats it as **ordinary**.

steps.text: Sit the sergeant exam next year
Keep putting 200 a month into shares
Keep running the gym's social media with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how progress works: some jobs change, people learn, the economy grows. At work I'd tell people to get ahead of it rather than complain. I'd say the force should buy what works and stop paying for forms nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for officers who use the tools and bad for those who don't. My driving and my first-on-scene work aren't going anywhere fast. The forms and approvals that drive me mad would finally get faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for any pilot of the new systems straight away. I'd still sit the sergeant exam, because a sergeant who understands the software is worth more. And I'd help Marco add an AI booking and coaching app to the gym, so he can take more members without hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Energised. Like someone finally fixed the slow bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Adding an AI coaching app means fewer coaches hired. Any doubt about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Marco's coach Dani is a friend. But if the gym down the road uses AI and we don't, we lose members and then everyone's job goes. That includes Dani's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat, who's 52 and still writes notes in a paper pocketbook. He's a great officer. I'd sit with him, but I wouldn't wait for him.

say: I'd say this is **how progress works**.
I'd tell colleagues to **get ahead** of it rather than complain.
think: Officers who **use the tools** win; those who don't lose out.
My **driving** and first-on-scene work aren't going anywhere fast.
do: Volunteer for **any pilot** of the new systems.
Help Marco add an **AI booking app** to the gym.
feel: **Energised**, as if the slow bits were finally fixed.

fieldNote: She frames change as **competition**: adopt or lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's adapt fast instead of trying to ban it. I'd say the government shouldn't freeze it, it should get out of the way and let people retrain. I'd post that, and I'd probably get shouted at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's harder than I'd say. The thinking part of my job goes in 2028, and then in 2031 robots can drive the pursuit car better than me. I'd be 31, and I've built my whole career plan on driving and making sergeant. A sergeant's job is mostly thinking, so that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the sergeant exam. I'd push hard on the gym with Marco, maybe a second small site, because people will still want a real person shouting at them to do one more squat. I'd move half my shares into cash for safety, and I'd look at private security firms that need people who can manage robot patrols.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd hide it. I'd be making plans out loud and worrying quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second gym site is a big bet in that world. Why there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because bodies are the last thing a robot replaces, at least in how people feel. If everyone's job gets stranger, people will want somewhere real to go at 6am. I'd bet our savings on that before I'd bet them on shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd publicly say get out of the way, but privately you're worried. Which is closer to the truth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I still don't think banning it works. But my own plan was built on the world staying slow, and I'm honest enough to say that scares me.

say: I'd say **adapt fast** instead of trying to ban it.
I'd say government should get out of the **way** and let people retrain.
think: The thinking part goes in **2028** and robots drive pursuits by **2031**.
My **sergeant plan** is mostly thinking work, so it goes first.
do: Open a **second gym site** with Marco.
Move **half my shares** into cash and look at private security firms.
feel: **Anxious** but hiding it, planning out loud and **worrying quietly**.
S2.quote: If everyone's job gets stranger, people will want somewhere real to go at 6am.
fieldNote: Clear gap between a **bold public line** and a private fear for her career.
She realises her **promotion plan** is thinking work and drops it fast.
She'd bet savings on the **gym** over shares, a telling shift.

steps.text: Open a second small gym site with Marco

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the fast one, I'd say adapt, don't ban. With five years I'd add that the force should let officers train for the new jobs now. I'd say it at work in a team meeting, not just online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a few good years of driving and maybe a few as a sergeant. I'd be 32 when the thinking work goes and around 35 when robots come for the driving. That's enough to build the gym properly and step across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit the sergeant exam, because a few years of a sergeant's pay helps. I'd do a part-time business course in the evenings in year one. And Marco and I would plan the second site for year three, not year one, with savings rather than a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the business course, if you already run the marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because marketing is the easy bit, and AI does most of it. I'd want to understand leases, staff and tax properly, because that's where small businesses die. Marco's great with members but hates paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss policing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The driving, mostly, and the team. But I'd rather leave policing on my own timing at 34 than be told at 35.

I'd say it in a **team meeting**, not just online.
think: Five years gives me some **driving** years and maybe a few as sergeant.
At **32 and 35** I'd have built the gym and stepped across.
do: Sit the **sergeant exam** for a few years of higher pay.

S3.quote: I'd rather leave policing on my own timing at 34 than be told at 35.
fieldNote: The extra time lets her keep **policing** and still plan an exit.

steps.text: Sit the sergeant exam for a few years of higher pay
Take an evening business course in leases, staff and tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. Maybe that's harsh, but I'd say it. At church I'd say it a bit more kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, I think. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and nearly 40 when robots come. That's a full career as a sergeant, maybe inspector, and a gym that's had ten years to grow. The thing I'd watch is whether AI coaching apps eat Marco's members before the robots ever come for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, nothing dramatic. Sit the sergeant exam, keep putting 200 a month into shares, and keep the gym's marketing going. We'd probably get married in a couple of years and look at buying a house instead of renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back, mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone who doesn't prepare has only themselves to blame. Would you say that to Pat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not to Pat's face. Pat's 52 and he'd be 62 by the time it lands, so ten years is a different thing for him. I'd sit with him, but I'd still say people have to help themselves first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Marco's gym the bigger worry in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, oddly. My job's safe for ten years, but a really good AI coach on your phone for five pounds a month could take the gym's newer members in two years. I'd make sure the gym does something an app can't, like classes where you actually know people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my career plan is built for a slower world and the gym would be our only safety net. What would help is cheap, fast business loans for small firms and a force that lets officers train for new roles on paid time. Not handouts, just room to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about driving. Everyone thinks it'll be the first thing robots take, but a pursuit at night in the rain is chaos. Still, I'd bet the robots get there, and I'd rather be the one selling the robots than the one chasing them.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the one selling the robots than the one chasing them.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old response driver** on the south side who uses AI every day.
She runs marketing for her boyfriend Marco's **gym**, which is the household's other income.
She believes in **markets and self-reliance**, and frames change as adopt or lose.
Fast AGI makes her drop **sergeant plans** and bet on the gym; slower worlds let her stay.
Her quiet worry is that **AI coaching apps** hit the gym before robots reach her.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her career plan assumes a slower world.
whatWouldHelp: Paid time for officers to **train** for new roles.
